title: Macareus. Ulixes et Circe
titleEn: Macareus; Ulysses and Circe — Metamorphoses XIV.223–319
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Macareus, one of Ulysses' men, tells what became of the crew: how Aeolus gave their leader the winds shut in an ox-hide, and how the companions, taking the bag for gold, opened it nine days out and were blown back; how Antiphates and the Laestrygonians stoned and sank every ship but one. Landing on Circe's shore, he warns Aeneas away from it, and describes how the lot sent him with Polites, Eurylochus, Elpenor and eighteen others up to her house, where a drugged cup and a touch of the wand turned them bristled and speechless and shut them in a sty. Eurylochus alone refused the cup; Ulysses came protected by the white flower moly, drove Circe back at swordpoint, and got his companions' bodies back as the price of a compact made in her chamber — and in the course of that year one of her maids began to tell Macareus about a marble statue that wears a woodpecker on its head.

sentences.t:
Aeolon ille refert Tusco regnare profundo,
Aeolon Hippotaden, cohibentem carcere ventos;
sentences.l: He relates that Aeolus reigns in the Tuscan deep, Aeolus the son of Hippotes, confining the winds in a prison;
sentences.i: He tells how Aeolus is king over the Tuscan sea — Aeolus son of Hippotes, who keeps the winds shut up in a prison.
sentences.n: Keep the frame straight from the first word. The “he” is Macareus, and 223–232 are his account given in indirect statement — accusative and infinitive, Aeolon ... regnare, “that Aeolus reigns” — so everything in these ten lines is his report, not the poem speaking. His direct speech begins at 233. Aeolon and Hippotaden are Greek accusatives; Hippotades is a patronymic, “son of Hippotes”. Cohibentem is a present participle agreeing with Aeolon, which the literal keeps as “confining”.

sentences.l: that the Dulichian leader took them, shut in an ox's hide — a gift worth remembering — and with a following blast went for nine days and caught sight of the land he had made for;
sentences.i: and how the leader from Dulichium received them shut in an ox-hide, a gift to be remembered, and ran nine days on a following wind and sighted the land he was making for.
sentences.n: Quos is a connecting relative picking up ventos from 224 — “and these”. The three perfect infinitives sumpsisse, isse and adspexisse continue the accusative and infinitive begun at 223, which is why the literal keeps them inside a “that” clause. Memorabile munus stands in apposition to quos, in the accusative. The “Dulichian leader” is Ulysses, named here only from an island of his kingdom; the periphrasis is Macareus's. Lucibus novem is an ablative of time; prose would normally put duration in the accusative, and the ablative here covers the nine days the run lasted, which is why the literal has “for nine days”. Luces, “lights”, is used for days. Petitam is the participle of peto, “sought for, made for”.

sentences.l: that, when the next dawn after the ninth was setting itself in motion, his companions, overcome by envy and by desire for plunder, reckoned it to be gold and took the bindings off the winds;
sentences.i: and how, when the tenth dawn was stirring, the crew, mastered by envy and greed for loot, took it for gold and stripped the fastenings off the winds.
sentences.n: Proxima post nonam aurora is the dawn next after the ninth, so the tenth — the count runs on from the nine days of 227. Sese moveret is reflexive, “was moving itself”, with cum and the imperfect subjunctive for the attendant circumstance. Victos agrees with socios and stays inside the indirect statement. Esse ratos is ratos esse, the perfect participle of the deponent reor with the infinitive: deponent, so active in force, “having reckoned”, and the literal keeps it active. Ligamina ventis is a dative of separation — the bindings taken off the winds, not given to them.

sentences.t:
cum quibus isse retro, per quas modo venerat undas,
Aeoliique ratem portus repetisse tyranni.
sentences.l: that with these the ship went back, through the waves over which it had just come, and sought again the harbour of the Aeolian tyrant.
sentences.i: and how the ship ran back with them over the very water it had just crossed, and came again to the harbour of the Aeolian king.
sentences.n: Cum quibus is another connecting relative, the winds again. The subject of both infinitives, isse in 231 and repetisse in 232, is ratem, which does not appear until 232 — the reader has to wait a line to learn what went back. Venerat is indicative inside the indirect statement: the relative clause is stated as fact rather than drawn into the report. Tyrannus is the Greek-derived word for a sole ruler and need not carry blame here; the literal keeps it flat.

sentences.t:
“Inde Lami veterem Laestrygonis” inquit “in urbem
venimus.
sentences.l: “From there,” he says, “we came into the ancient city of Lamus the Laestrygonian.
sentences.i: “From there,” he says, “we came to the old city of Lamus the Laestrygonian.
sentences.n: Direct speech begins here, and from 233 to the end of these lines Macareus speaks in his own voice; the poem's indirect report is over. Inquit interrupts the sentence and the edition closes and reopens the quotation marks around it: Lami veterem Laestrygonis stands before it and in urbem after it, so the noun is cut off from its adjective and its genitive by the interruption. Lami is a genitive depending on urbem and Laestrygonis is in apposition to Lami; the lines say only that the city is Lamus the Laestrygonian's, and nothing more about him.

sentences.t: Antiphates terra regnabat in illa.
sentences.l: Antiphates was reigning in that land.
sentences.i: Antiphates was king in that land.
sentences.n: The imperfect regnabat sets the standing state of affairs behind the action that follows. The prepositional phrase in illa terra is split around the verb, terra ... in illa, a displacement verse allows freely.

sentences.t:
Missus ad hunc ego sum, numero comitante duorum,
vixque fuga quaesita salus comitique mihique:
sentences.l: I was sent to him, with a number of two accompanying, and safety was barely got by flight, both for my companion and for me:
sentences.i: I was the one sent to him, and two men went with me; my companion and I barely came away alive, by running:
sentences.n: Numero comitante duorum is an ablative absolute, literally “with a number of two accompanying”, a periphrasis for “with two companions”, and the literal keeps the absolute. Comiti and mihi are datives of advantage. The singular comiti already gives away that only one of the two came back with him; the next unit says what happened to the other. The colon points forward to that explanation.

sentences.t:
tertius e nobis Laestrygonis impia tinxit
ora cruore suo.
sentences.l: the third of us stained the Laestrygonian's unholy mouth with his own blood.
sentences.i: the third of us dyed that unholy Laestrygonian mouth red with his own blood.
sentences.n: The victim is the grammatical subject and suo refers to him: the man who was eaten is made the agent of the staining, a grim inversion the literal keeps rather than turning it round into “his blood stained”. Tinxit is “dipped, dyed”. Ora is the plural of os used of a single mouth, which verse does regularly.

sentences.t:
Fugientibus instat et agmen
concitat Antiphates.
sentences.l: Antiphates presses hard on those fleeing and rouses up a column.
sentences.i: Antiphates comes on hard after the runaways and calls out the host.
sentences.n: Fugientibus is a dative with insto, “press upon”, and a present participle used as a noun, “those fleeing” — the literal keeps it as a participle rather than a clause. Instat and concitat are historic presents after the perfect tinxit, which closes 237: the narrative shifts into the present exactly at the moment of pursuit. The subject Antiphates is held back behind both verbs and arrives only as the second word of 239, after concitat.

sentences.t:
Coeunt et saxa trabesque
coniciunt merguntque viros merguntque carinas.
sentences.l: They come together and hurl rocks and beams, and sink men and sink keels.
sentences.i: They mass together and throw down rocks and tree-trunks, and they sink the men and they sink the ships.
sentences.n: Coeunt is co-eunt, “go together”. The repeated merguntque ... merguntque makes the two sinkings one motion instead of two events, and the piled connectives — et, then three -que — keep the lines from pausing. Carinas, “keels”, stands for the whole ships.

sentences.t:
Una tamen, quae nos ipsumque vehebat Ulixen,
effugit.
sentences.l: One, however — the one that was carrying us and Ulysses himself — escaped.
sentences.i: One ship, though, got away: the one carrying us and Ulysses himself.
sentences.n: Una is feminine and agrees with a noun that is never expressed: after carinas in 240 the reader supplies navis or ratis, and the vessel is identified only by its number and by who was aboard. Ulixen is the Greek accusative.

sentences.t:
Amissa sociorum parte dolentes
multaque conquesti terris adlabimur illis,
quas procul hinc cernis (procul hinc, mihi crede, videnda
insula, visa mihi!),
sentences.l: Grieving, with a part of our companions lost, and having lamented much, we glide up to those lands which you make out far from here (far from here, believe me, is that island to be looked at — it has been looked at by me!),
sentences.i: Sick at heart, with part of our company gone, and after much lamenting, we came gliding in to that country you can make out away over there — far off is where you should look at that island, believe me: I have looked at it —
sentences.n: Amissa ... parte is an ablative absolute, “with a part lost”, and conquesti is the perfect participle of the deponent conqueror, active in force; adlabimur is likewise deponent and active, “we glide up to”, with the dative terris illis. The aside turns on two forms of the same verb: videnda is the gerundive of obligation, “to be looked at”, and visa is the plain perfect participle, “looked at” — the island is one you should view from a distance, and he knows because he has viewed it. Line 244 carries procul hinc twice; at the second, inside the parenthesis, Magnus prints procul hinc while some editions read procul est, “far off is the island that is to be looked at”.

sentences.t:
tuque o iustissime Troum,
nate dea (neque enim finito Marte vocandus
hostis es, Aenea), moneo, fuge litora Circes.
sentences.l: and you, o most just of the Trojans, born of a goddess (for, the war being finished, you are not to be called an enemy, Aeneas), I warn you: flee the shores of Circe.
sentences.i: And you, most upright of the Trojans, goddess-born — now that the war is over you are not to be called an enemy, Aeneas — I warn you: keep away from Circe's shore.
sentences.n: Macareus breaks off his narrative to address Aeneas directly, and holds the name back: “most just of the Trojans” at 245, “born of a goddess” at 246, and only at 247 the vocative Aenea. Nate dea is the vocative of the participle with a bare ablative of origin, “born from a goddess”. Finito Marte is an ablative absolute with the god's name standing for the war he governs, and the literal keeps the absolute. Vocandus es is the gerundive of obligation, “you are not to be called”. Circes is the Greek genitive of Circe — the first time she is named.

sentences.l: We too, with the pine moored on the Circean shore, mindful of Antiphates and of the untamed Cyclops, refused to go, or to enter houses we did not know;
sentences.i: We too, once the ship was tied up on Circe's shore, with Antiphates and the savage Cyclops in mind, said no to going, no to walking into a house we did not know.
sentences.n: Religata ... pinu is an ablative absolute, “with the pine moored”, and pinu is the tree standing for the ship built of it — the second such substitution here after carinas at 240. Memores takes the genitive, Antiphatae and Cyclopis. Negabamus with the infinitives ire and subire is “we refused to go”, not “we denied that we went”. The Cyclops belongs to what these men have already been through, not to anything told in these lines.

sentences.t:
sorte sumus lecti, sors me fidumque Politen
Eurylochumque simul nimiique Elpenora vini
bisque novem socios Circaea ad moenia misit.
sentences.l: by lot we were chosen; the lot sent me, and faithful Polites, and Eurylochus with us, and Elpenor of too much wine, and twice nine companions, to the Circean walls.
sentences.i: We were picked by lot; the lot sent me, and loyal Polites, and Eurylochus along with us, and Elpenor, who liked his wine too well, and eighteen more, up to Circe's walls.
sentences.n: The same noun stands in two cases in successive clauses of one line: sorte, the ablative of means by which they were chosen, then sors, the nominative that does the sending. Nimii vini is a genitive of description attached to Elpenor, “of too much wine”, and the literal keeps the genitive rather than turning it into a clause. Bis novem is verse arithmetic for eighteen, so with the four men named the party is twenty-two.

sentences.t:
Quae simul attigimus stetimusque in limine tecti,
mille lupi mixtaeque lupis ursique leaeque
occursu fecere metum, sed nulla timenda
nullaque erat nostro factura in corpore vulnus.
sentences.l: As soon as we reached them and stood on the threshold of the house, a thousand wolves, and bears and lionesses mingled with the wolves, made fear by running to meet us; but none was to be feared, and none was going to make a wound in our body.
sentences.i: The moment we reached the walls and stood at the door of the house, a thousand wolves — and bears and lionesses mixed in among them — put fear into us as they ran up; but not one of them was to be feared, not one was going to leave a wound on us.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative picking up Circaea moenia from 253, and simul here is simul ac, “as soon as”. Fecere is fecerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere, the ordinary verse alternative to -erunt; you will meet it again two lines on, at movere in 258. The last clause sets two verbal adjectives against each other: timenda is a gerundive of obligation, what ought to be feared, and factura a future participle, what would actually have happened — the literal keeps the difference as “was to be feared” against “was going to make”. Magnus prints ursique, masculine bears; some editions print ursaeque, she-bears, to match the feminine leaeque beside it.

sentences.t:
Quin etiam blandas movere per aera caudas
nostraque adulantes comitant vestigia, donec
excipiunt famulae perque atria marmore tecta
ad dominam ducunt:
sentences.l: Nay more, they moved coaxing tails through the air, and, fawning, they attend our footsteps, until maidservants take us over and lead us through halls roofed with marble to their mistress:
sentences.i: More than that: they swung their tails at us to charm us, and came fawning along at our heels, until serving-women took us in hand and led us through marble-panelled halls to their mistress:
sentences.n: Movere is again the -ere perfect, moverunt, and it stands beside the present comitant in the same sentence: the perfect for the one gesture, the present for the fawning that goes on all the way to the door. Adulantes is the participle of the deponent adulor, active in force, “fawning”. Comitant is the rare active of the usually deponent comitor. Blandas describes the tails themselves, the beasts' coaxing carried over to the thing that does the coaxing. Note tecta at 260, the participle “roofed”, against tecti at 254, the noun “house”: the same stem, two different words, six lines apart.

sentences.t:
pulchro sedet illa recessu,
sollemni solio, pallamque induta nitentem
insuper aurato circumvelatur amictu.
sentences.l: she sits in a lovely recess, on a ceremonial throne, and, having put on a shining robe, is veiled over it with a gilded mantle.
sentences.i: There she sits in a beautiful alcove, on a throne of state; she has put on a gleaming robe, and over it she is wrapped in a mantle worked with gold.
sentences.n: Pallam induta is the pattern to learn here: a perfect passive participle used in the middle sense, “having clothed herself”, taking a direct accusative — the Greek accusative construction, and the literal renders it actively for that reason. Circumvelatur is passive in form and can be read either as a true passive, “is veiled about”, or in the same middle sense, “wraps herself about”; the literal keeps the passive and the question is genuinely open. Sollemnis means “belonging to the established rite”, so a throne of state rather than merely a grand one.

sentences.t:
Nereides nymphaeque simul, quae vellera motis
nulla trahunt digitis nec fila sequentia ducunt:
sentences.l: Nereids and nymphs together, who draw out no fleeces with moving fingers nor lead out threads that follow after:
sentences.i: Nereids and nymphs are there with her — who card no fleece with busy fingers and spin out no following thread:
sentences.n: The main clause here has no verb: the only verbs in the unit, trahunt and ducunt, belong to the relative clause. Nereides nymphaeque is a nominative left hanging at the colon, and its own verbs, disponunt and secernunt, come only in the next unit at 266 and 267; the literal keeps the fragment rather than inventing “there are”. Two noun-adjective pairs are interlocked across the line-end: vellera and motis stand at the end of 264 while their partners nulla and digitis follow in 265. Vellera trahere and fila ducere are the ordinary terms for working wool, so the line says what these attendants do not do before the next says what they do.

sentences.t:
gramina disponunt sparsosque sine ordine flores
secernunt calathis variasque coloribus herbas;
sentences.l: they lay out grasses in order, and sort into baskets the flowers scattered without arrangement, and the herbs various in their colours;
sentences.i: they set the grasses out in rows, and pick apart into baskets the flowers strewn at random, and the plants of many colours;
sentences.n: Disponunt is dis-ponunt, “place apart, arrange in order”, and it answers sine ordine in the same line: what the flowers lack, these women supply. Calathis may be a dative of direction, which verse allows, or an ablative of place — “into baskets” or “in baskets” — and nothing here decides it. Varias coloribus is an ablative of respect, “various as to their colours”, which the literal keeps.

sentences.t:
ipsa quod hae faciunt opus, exigit, ipsa, quis usus
quove sit in folio, quae sit concordia mixtis,
novit et advertens pensas examinat herbas.
sentences.l: She herself exacts the work these women do; she herself knows what use there is, and in which leaf it lies, and what agreement there is for things mixed, and, turning her attention to them, she tests on the balance the herbs already weighed out.
sentences.i: She herself calls for the work they do; she herself knows what each is good for, and in which leaf the power lies, and what mixtures agree; and she gives her mind to it and checks the weighed herbs on the scales.
sentences.n: Ipsa opens 268 and ipsa stands again in the same line, just after exigit, both of them Circe: the maids do the work, the knowledge is hers and nobody else's. Novit governs three indirect questions — quis usus, quove in folio, quae concordia — with the subjunctive sit written twice and understood in the first, which is why the literal keeps them as questions inside the clause rather than flattening them into nouns. Mixtis is a dative, “for things mixed together”. The last clause weighs twice over: pensas is “weighed out”, from pendo, and examinat is “tests on the balance”, from examen, the tongue of a pair of scales.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi nos vidit, dicta acceptaque salute,
diffudit vultus et reddidit omina voce.
sentences.l: When she saw us, with a greeting spoken and received, she spread her face open and gave back words of good omen with her voice.
sentences.i: When she saw us — greetings given and returned — her face opened into a smile, and she answered with words of good omen.
sentences.n: Haec is the demonstrative used as a connective, “and she”: Circe, carried over from illa at 261. Dicta acceptaque salute is a single ablative absolute with two participles sharing one noun, and the literal keeps the absolute rather than turning it into “after they had greeted each other”. Diffudit vultus is literally “spread out her face”, the muscles unclenching into a smile; vultus is accusative plural for the one face. Omina are words that carry an omen, so reddidit omina voce is a formal way of saying she answered with words of good augury. Magnus prints voce, “with her voice”; some editions print votis, “with good wishes”.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, misceri tosti iubet hordea grani
mellaque vimque meri cum lacte coagula passo,
quique sub hac lateant furtim dulcedine, sucos
adicit.
sentences.l: No delay: she orders barley of roasted grain to be mixed, and honey, and the force of neat wine, and curds with milk left to thicken; and she adds juices, such as would lurk secretly beneath this sweetness.
sentences.i: No delay: she has them mix roasted barley-meal, honey, strong unwatered wine and curds with thickened milk — and she slips in juices of the sort that hide unnoticed under all that sweetness.
sentences.n: Nec mora is a verbless formula, “and no delay”. Misceri is a passive infinitive after iubet, which the literal keeps: she orders the mixture to be made, she does not stir it. Vis meri is the strength of the unmixed wine. Lacte passo is milk with the participle of pando, “spread out”, used of things left in the sun to dry, so milk allowed to stand and thicken; the phrase cum lacte coagula passo is compressed and the exact preparation is not certain. In the last clause the relative comes before its antecedent: quique ... lateant is a subjunctive relative clause of the characterising sort, and the noun it belongs to, sucos, only arrives at the end of 275, with the verb adicit left alone at the head of 276. Macareus is telling this long afterwards, and furtim gives away what the men at the table could not see.

sentences.t: Accipimus sacra data pocula dextra.
sentences.l: We take the cups given by her holy right hand.
sentences.i: We took the cups her holy right hand held out to us.
sentences.n: Sacra dextra is an ablative, “by the holy right hand”. Sacer means “consecrated”, and so “holy”, but it can also mean “set apart, accursed”, and one line after furtim a reader may hear either; the literal keeps “holy” and leaves the edge where the Latin leaves it. Accipimus is present, continuing the historic presents iubet and adicit.

sentences.t:
Quae simul arenti sitientes hausimus ore,
et tetigit summos virga dea dira capillos,
(et pudet et referam!) saetis horrescere coepi
nec iam posse loqui, pro verbis edere raucum
murmur et in terram toto procumbere vultu;
sentences.l: As soon as we, thirsty, had drained them with a dry mouth, and the dread goddess had touched the tops of our hair with her wand — I am ashamed of it, and I shall tell it! — I began to bristle with stiff hairs, and no longer to be able to speak, to put out a hoarse grunt in place of words, and to sink forward on the ground with my whole face;
sentences.i: The moment we drank them down, parched, with dry mouths, and the terrible goddess touched the top of our hair with her wand — I am ashamed of it, and I will tell it — I began to bristle with coarse hair, to lose the power of speech, to push out a hoarse grunt instead of words, and to go down face first on the ground;
sentences.n: One verb carries the whole transformation: coepi at the end of 279 governs four infinitives strung out to 281 — horrescere, posse, edere, procumbere — so the change is one continuous beginning rather than four events, and the literal keeps the chain rather than breaking it into sentences. Et pudet et referam is a correlative pair, “both it shames me and I shall tell it”. The form referam could in itself be a deliberative subjunctive, “am I to tell it?”, but et ... et pairs it with the indicative pudet, so it is the future indicative and a promise rather than a question. Saetis is an ablative of means with horrescere, and saetae are the stiff hairs of a pig: the word performs the change before anything names the animal. The wand, virga, comes back twice more, at 295 and reversed at 300.

sentences.t:
osque meum sensi pando occallescere rostro,
colla tumere toris, et qua modo pocula parte
sumpta mihi fuerant, illa vestigia feci,
sentences.l: and I felt my mouth harden into a broad snout, and my neck swell with thick muscle; and with the part with which the cups had just been taken by me, with that part I made footprints,
sentences.i: and I felt my mouth harden into a broad snout and my neck thicken with muscle; and the hand that had just taken the cup was now what I printed the ground with,
sentences.n: Sensi governs two infinitives, occallescere in 282 and tumere in 283, and the literal keeps both under “I felt”. The last clause puts the relative before its correlative — qua ... parte, then illa — and draws the noun parte into the relative clause; the periphrasis avoids saying “hand”, because he no longer has one. Sumpta fuerant uses fuerant rather than erant for the passive, giving a state completed and over, and mihi is the dative of the agent, which the literal renders “by me”. Vestigia feci is “I made footprints”, that is, walked on it.

sentences.t:
cumque eadem passis (tantum medicamina possunt!)
claudor hara, solumque suis caruisse figura
vidimus Eurylochum:
sentences.l: and together with those who had suffered the same things — so much can drugs do! — I am shut in a sty; and we saw that Eurylochus alone had lacked the shape that belonged to his own men:
sentences.i: and along with the others who had gone through the same thing — such is the power of drugs — I was shut in a pigsty; and we saw that Eurylochus alone had not taken on the shape the rest of us wore:
sentences.n: Passis is the ablative plural after cum, the participle of the deponent patior, active in force and governing the accusative eadem, “together with those having suffered the same things”, and the literal keeps it active. Claudor is a present standing among perfects — sensi, feci, vidimus — so the moment of being shut in is held in front of the reader instead of being reported. The last clause is compressed: careo takes the ablative figura, and suis goes with it as a dative, “the shape belonging to his own men”, so that what Eurylochus alone lacked was the shape his companions now had. Suis could in form be the genitive singular of sus, “of a pig”, which would give “lacked a pig's shape” — but the metre rules that out. Scanned foot by foot, 286 runs dactyl, spondee, dactyl, dactyl, dactyl and close, and the fourth foot opens on the -is of suis, which must therefore be long; the genitive singular of sus has a short i, while the dative and ablative plural of suus has a long one. Hara is a pigsty, and the animal itself is never named in these lines — only saetae at 279 and 303, hara here, and pecus saetigerum at 288 and 289.

sentences.t: solus data pocula fugit.
sentences.l: he alone fled the cups that were given.
sentences.i: he alone had escaped the cups when they were handed round.
sentences.n: Fugit here is the perfect fugit with a long first syllable, not the present with a short one: the sixth foot needs a long syllable at the start, and the line scans vi-di-mus / Eu-ry-lo- / chum so- / lus da-ta / po-cu-la / fu-git, dactyl, dactyl, spondee, dactyl, dactyl, close — so the tense is settled by the metre. Fugio here takes an accusative object, “fled the cups”, which means he would not take them. Data pocula repeats the phrase of 276, marking these as the same cups the rest of them accepted; the cups are called treacherous when they come round again at 294 and 295.

sentences.t:
Quae nisi vitasset, pecoris pars una manerem
nunc quoque saetigeri, nec tantae cladis ab illo
certior ad Circen ultor venisset Ulixes.
sentences.l: And if he had not avoided them, I should still now be remaining one part of the bristly herd, nor would Ulysses have come to Circe as an avenger, made certain by him of so great a disaster.
sentences.i: If he had not dodged them, I would still be one head of that bristly herd today, and Ulysses would never have come to Circe as an avenger, told by him how great the disaster was.
sentences.n: One condition holds two different unrealities. The protasis vitasset is pluperfect subjunctive, a past that did not happen; the first apodosis manerem is imperfect subjunctive with nunc quoque, a present that is not so; the second, venisset, is pluperfect again. The literal keeps all three tenses distinct — “if he had not avoided”, “I should still be remaining”, “would have come”. Quae is a connecting relative, the cups of 287. Pars una pecoris is literally “one part of the herd”, which the literal keeps; the idiomatic gives the ordinary English of it, “one head”. Pecoris in 288 waits for its adjective saetigeri, which is the third word of 289. Certior with the genitive tantae cladis is the idiom for being informed of something, with ab illo — Eurylochus — for the source.

sentences.t:
Pacifer huic dederat florem Cyllenius album,
moly vocant superi, nigra radice tenetur;
sentences.l: The peace-bringing Cyllenian had given him a white flower; moly the gods above call it; it is held fast by a black root.
sentences.i: The peace-bringer of Cyllene had given him a white flower — moly, the gods above call it — held down by a black root.
sentences.n: Pacifer Cyllenius names the god by an epithet, “peace-bringing”, and by his mountain, Cyllene; the name Mercurius is not used anywhere in these lines. Huic is Ulysses, the last person named, at the end of 290 — not Eurylochus, who was ab illo in 289. The clause moly vocant superi is dropped in without brackets or a connective, and it credits the name to the superi, the gods above, giving no mortal name at all. Tenetur is “is held fast”, the plant's grip on the ground: the flower white above and the root black below.

sentences.t:
tutus eo monitisque simul caelestibus intrat
ille domum Circes, et ad insidiosa vocatus
pocula, conantem virga mulcere capillos
reppulit et stricto pavidam deterruit ense.
sentences.l: Safe by it and by the heavenly warnings together, he enters the house of Circe; and, called to the treacherous cups, he thrust her back as she was trying to stroke his hair with the wand, and with sword drawn frightened her off, trembling.
sentences.i: Protected by the flower and by the god's instructions together, he went into Circe's house; and when he was called to the treacherous cup, he shoved her back as she tried to pass the wand over his hair, and drew his sword and drove her off in terror.
sentences.n: Tutus takes the ablative of means, eo, “safe by means of it”, the moly. Vocatus is the perfect passive participle, “having been called”. The object of reppulit is not a pronoun at all but the bare participle conantem, “her trying”; conantem has one form for either gender, and it is pavidam in 296 that first marks the gender grammatically — though domum Circes in 294 has already told the reader whose house this is. Stricto ense may be an ablative absolute, “the sword having been drawn”, or a plain instrumental, “with the drawn sword”; the literal keeps a form that leaves both open. Pavidam does the work of a clause: she is now the frightened one. The wand does not change hands, though — she is still wielding it at 300.

sentences.t:
Inde fides dextraeque datae, thalamoque receptus
coniugii dotem sociorum corpora poscit.
sentences.l: Thereupon a pledge was given, and right hands; and, received into the marriage-chamber, he demands the bodies of his companions as the dowry of the union.
sentences.i: After that a pledge was made and right hands exchanged; and, taken into her bed, he demanded his companions' bodies as the dowry of the match.
sentences.n: The clasping of right hands is the gesture that seals a compact, and the plural participle datae takes fides and dextrae together under one verb. Receptus is passive: he is the one received into the chamber, and she is the one who receives him. The lines set four steps in order — the drawn sword of 296, then the pledge, then the bed, then the demand. Dos is what a bride brings to a marriage, so calling his companions' bodies the dowry of this union inverts the term: the bridegroom names the price and collects it. Note where the narrator is: he told us at 286 that he was shut in a sty, and he is still there until 299; at this point he does not say how he knows what happened inside the house, and the nearest he comes to it is 309, where he says only that over the year he saw much and heard much.

sentences.t:
Spargimur ignotae sucis melioribus herbae
percutimurque caput conversae verbere virgae,
verbaque dicuntur dictis contraria verbis.
sentences.l: We are sprinkled with the better juices of a plant unknown to us, and we are struck as to the head with a stroke of the wand turned about, and words are spoken contrary to the words that had been spoken.
sentences.i: We were sprinkled with the better juices of a plant we did not know, and struck on the head with a stroke of the wand turned the other way, and words were spoken that ran backwards against the words spoken before.
sentences.n: Percutimur caput is the Greek accusative of respect with a passive verb, “we are struck as to the head”, and the literal keeps it in that shape; compare pallam induta at 262, where an accusative is likewise retained beside a middle participle. All three verbs here are passive — spargimur, percutimur, dicuntur — so the men are done to throughout, and no agent is named. Sucis melioribus answers the sucos of 275: the same kind of thing undoes what it did, as the reversed wand undoes what the wand did at 278 and 295. The last line reverses in its grammar as well as its sense: verba and verbis, the same noun in two cases, with dicuntur and dictis from the same verb beside them.

sentences.t:
Quo magis illa canit, magis hoc tellure levati
erigimur, saetaeque cadunt, bifidosque relinquit
rima pedes, redeunt umeri et subiecta lacertis
bracchia sunt:
sentences.l: By how much the more she chants, by so much the more, lifted from the ground, are we raised upright; and the bristles fall; and the cleft leaves our two-parted feet; the shoulders come back, and forearms are set under the upper arms:
sentences.i: The more she chanted, the more we came up off the ground and stood straight; the bristles dropped away; the split left our cloven feet; shoulders came back, and forearms were fitted under upper arms:
sentences.n: Quo ... hoc are ablatives of measure of difference in correlation, “by how much ... by so much”, and the literal keeps the doubling rather than smoothing it to “the more ... the more”. Tellure levati is an ablative of separation with the participle, “lifted from the earth”. The third clause inverts the expected subject: rima, the split itself, is made to leave the feet, rather than the feet losing their split. Latin distinguishes the upper arm, lacertus, from the forearm, bracchium, and subiecta sunt is a perfect passive — the parts are fitted back under one another, not growing of themselves.

sentences.t:
flentem flentes amplectimur ipsi
haeremusque ducis collo nec verba locuti
ulla priora sumus quam nos testantia gratos.
sentences.l: weeping ourselves, we embrace him as he weeps, and we cling to our leader's neck, nor did we speak any words earlier than words testifying that we were grateful.
sentences.i: Weeping ourselves, we put our arms round him as he wept, and hung on our leader's neck, and the first words we spoke were words of thanks.
sentences.n: Flentem flentes sets the same participle in two cases side by side, accusative then nominative, and the word is deliberately not varied: he weeps and they weep, in one phrase. Collo with haeremus is most naturally a dative, “cling to the neck”, though an ablative of place is possible. Locuti ... sumus is the perfect of the deponent loquor, active in force, and its auxiliary is held over the line-end: locuti closes 306 and sumus stands in 307. Nec ... ulla priora ... quam is a comparative way of saying that thanks came before anything else; testantia governs the accusative and infinitive nos gratos, with esse left out.

sentences.t:
Annua nos illic tenuit mora, multaque praesens
tempore tam longo vidi, multa auribus hausi,
hoc quoque cum multis, quod clam mihi rettulit una
quattuor e famulis ad talia sacra paratis.
sentences.l: A year-long delay held us there, and, being present myself, I saw many things in so long a time, and many I drained in with my ears — this too among many, which one of the four maidservants, made ready for such rites, secretly told me.
sentences.i: A whole year's stay kept us there, and in so long a time I saw much for myself and took in much by ear — this among the rest, which one of the four serving-women trained for such rites told me on the quiet.
sentences.n: Annua opens the line and its noun mora closes the clause, with the whole statement standing between them. Praesens is “present in person”, and it is set against auribus hausi: what Macareus saw for himself against what only reached him as report — which matters, because the tale that follows is of the second kind. Hausi is the same verb used of draining the cups at 277, so hearing is drinking here too. Una quattuor e famulis is “one out of the four”, and ad talia sacra paratis is a dative plural with famulis, “made ready for such rites”. This maid is the new speaker: from 318 the words are hers.

sentences.t:
Cum duce namque meo Circe dum sola moratur,
illa mihi niveo factum de marmore signum
ostendit iuvenale, gerens in vertice picum,
aede sacra positum multisque insigne coronis.
sentences.l: For while Circe was lingering alone with my leader, she showed me a youthful statue made of snow-white marble, carrying a woodpecker on its crown, set in a holy shrine and marked out by many garlands.
sentences.i: For while Circe was off alone with my leader, she showed me a statue of a young man made of snow-white marble, with a woodpecker on his head, standing in a holy shrine and singled out by many wreaths.
sentences.n: Dum takes the present indicative moratur even of past time, which is why the literal has to render it “was lingering”. De niveo marmore is de with the ablative of material. Gerens has one form for a nominative feminine, which would agree with illa, the maid, and for a neuter accusative, which agrees with signum; the sense settles it, and so does the company it keeps, since factum, iuvenale, positum and insigne all agree with signum. It is the statue that carries the bird, not the maid who is speaking. Picus is the woodpecker; the statue's name has not been given yet, and the maid's answer, which begins at 318, is offered as the explanation of the bird.

sentences.t:
Quis foret et quare sacra coleretur in aede,
cur hanc ferret avem, quaerenti et scire volenti
“accipe” ait “Macareu, dominaeque potentia quae sit
hinc quoque disce meae:
sentences.l: To me, asking and wanting to know who he was, and why he was worshipped in a holy shrine, and why he carried this bird, she says: “Take it in, Macareus, and learn from this too what my mistress's power is:
sentences.i: I asked, and wanted to know, who he was, and why he was worshipped in a holy shrine, and why he carried that bird; and she said: “Listen, Macareus, and learn from this too what my mistress can do:
sentences.n: Three indirect questions — quis foret, quare coleretur, cur ferret — all hang on quaerenti, and all take the imperfect subjunctive, foret being the alternative form for esset. Quaerenti and volenti are datives with no pronoun beside them: the “me” has to be supplied, and only the vocative Macareu in 318 tells us whose datives they are. Macareu is a Greek vocative in -eu. The frame is now three deep: the poem reports Macareus in 223–232, Macareus speaks in the first person from 233, and a maidservant speaks inside that from 318. The edition marks her speech with the same double quotation marks it used for his at 233 and does not distinguish the inner level; the only closing marks in these lines are the ones that let inquit at 233 and ait at 318 stand outside the quotation, and Macareus's own speech is never closed. Dominae, the fourth word of 318, waits for its possessive meae, which comes only in 319.

sentences.t: tu dictis adice mentem!
sentences.l: do you apply your mind to my words!”
sentences.i: give my words your attention!”
sentences.n: Adice mentem is “put your mind to it”, with dictis as the dative. The pronoun tu is not needed for the sense and marks the turn from what she promises to what she requires. The part stops at the end of 319, which is a complete verse, with the maid's story still ahead of her.
